questions.q_en: In which century did large-scale building activity begin under the Delhi Sultanate?
questions.solution_en:
Although by the eighth century CE, Muslims had begun to construct in Sind, Gujarat, etc., it was only in the early thirteenth century that large-scale building activity begun under the Delhi Sultanate, established after the Turkish conquest of northern India.

Large-scale building activity under the Delhi Sultanate began in the early 13th century CE after the establishment of the Sultanate in 1206 CE. The Slave Dynasty (Mamluk Dynasty), particularly under rulers like Qutb-ud-din Aibak and Iltutmish, initiated major construction projects, including:

• Qutb Minar (started by Qutb-ud-din Aibak in 1199, completed by Iltutmish)

• Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (first mosque built in Delhi)

• Early fortifications and tombs

questions.q_en: Which architectural form was introduced by Muslims that enabled spanning of large spaces without pillars?
questions.solution_en:
• Arcuate form refers to the use of arches, domes, and vaults, which were introduced by Muslim architects in India. This style allowed for the spanning of large spaces without the need for many pillars, unlike the traditional Indian trabeate (post-and-lintel) system.

• Trabeation is the older Indian method of construction using horizontal beams (lintels) supported by vertical columns, seen in temples.

• Stellate form refers to star-shaped designs, not a structural technique.

• Chevron pattern is a decorative zigzag motif, not a construction style.

questions.q_en:
Identify the incorrect statement.

A. Gol Gumbad is situated in Bijapur in the Bijapur District of Andhra Pradesh.

B. It is the mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah.
questions.solution_en:
• Gol Gumbad(also written as Gol Gumbaz) is situated in Bijapur in the Bijapur District of Karnataka.

• It is the mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah (1626 - 1656), the seventh Sultan of the Adil Shahi Dynasty of Bijapur (1489 - 1686).

• Built by the ruler himself, it is a striking edifice in spite of being unfinished.

• The tomb is a complex of buildings such as a gateway, a Naqqar Khana, a mosque and a sarai located within a large-walled garden.

• The Gumbad is a monumental square building topped with a circular drum over which rests a majestic dome, giving the building its nomenclature.

• It is built of dark gray basalt and decorated plasterwork. Each wall of the tomb is one hundred and thirty-five feet long and one hundred and ten feet high and ten feet thick.

• With the drum and the dome, the building rises to a height of over two hundred feet.

• The tomb has only one square chamber and the dome, with a diameter of one hundred and twenty-five feet, it covers an uninterrupted floor space of 18,337 square feet, the second largest in the world.

questions.q_en: What is the height of each side of the Taj Mahal from floor to roof and roof to pinnacle?
questions.solution_en:
All sides of the building, the twin elevations of floor to roof and roof to pinnacle, atop the foliated crest of the dome, measure 186 feet each.

Further information:

• Taj Mahal was built in Agra by Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for his deceased wife Mumtaz Mahal

• From 1632 onwards it took nearly twenty years and 20,000 specialised workers to complete this monument.

• The tomb is laid out in a Chahar Bagh, criss-crossed with paths and water courses, interspersed with pools and fountains.

• At the corners of the terrace stand four tall, tapering minarets, one hundred and thirty-two feet high.

• Four types of embellishments have been used with great effect for the interior and exterior surfaces of the Taj Mahal.

• These are stone carvings in high and low relief on the walls, the delicate carving of marble into jalis and graceful volutes, and the creation of arabesques with pietra dura on walls and tombstones and geometric designs with tessellation.

• Lastly, the art of calligraphy is used with the inlay of jasper in white marble to write Quranic verses.

• Marble for the building was quarried from the Makrana mines in Rajasthan and this white edifice is contrasted with the red sandstone of the surrounding structures.

• Marble for the building was quarried from the Makrana mines in Rajasthan and this white edifice is contrasted with the red sandstone of the surrounding structures.

• The tomb structure is a square with chamfers forming eight sides, recessed with deep arches.

questions.q_en: What feature made arches in Mughal architecture distinctive from the 16th century onwards?
questions.solution_en:
From the sixteenth century onwards arches were designed with trefoil or multiple foliations.

• Trefoil (three-lobed) or multiple foliations (cusps) - These ornate, curved designs became a hallmark of Mughal arches, seen in structures like the Buland Darwaza (Fatehpur Sikri) and Humayun's Tomb.

• Keystone designs - While keystones were structurally important, they weren't unique to Mughal arches.

• Chevron patterning - A decorative zigzag motif, not a defining feature of Mughal arches.

• Buttress supports - Used for stability but not specific to Mughal arch aesthetics.

questions.q_en: Which decorative technique involved the use of yellow marble, jade and jasper on walls and tombstones?
questions.solution_en:
Pietra dura (or parchin kari) was a decorative inlay technique widely used in Mughal architecture, involving the precise cutting and fitting of semi-precious stones (such as yellow marble, jade, jasper, lapis lazuli, and carnelian) into marble surfaces. This technique was prominently featured in:

• Taj Mahal (floral motifs on walls and tombstones)

• Red Fort (Delhi) and Itmad-ud-Daulah's Tomb

Further information:

• Intaglio - A carving technique where designs are incised into the surface, not inlaid.

• Arabesque - Intricate scrollwork or floral patterns, typically carved or painted, not inlaid.

• Encaustic tile work - Glazed colored tiles, not stone inlay.

questions.q_en: What is the Chahar Bagh style used in Mughal architecture?
options_en: A formal garden layout divided into four sections
questions.solution_en:
The Chahar Bagh (meaning "four gardens" in Persian) is a classic Mughal garden design based on symmetry and the concept of paradise gardens.

Key features include:

• Division into four quadrants by walkways or water channels.

• Central water features (e.g., fountains, pools) reflecting Islamic notions of paradise.

• Examples: Taj Mahal's gardens, Shalimar Bagh (Kashmir), Humayun's Tomb complex.

questions.q_en: What type of structure was a Sarai in medieval India?
questions.solution_en:
• A hugely interesting feature of medieval India was the sarais which ringed cities and dotted the vast space of the Indian subcontinent.

• Sarais were largely built on a simple square or rectangular plan and were meant to provide temporary accommodation to Indian and foreign travellers, pilgrims, merchants, traders, etc. In effect, sarais were public domains which thronged with people of varied cultural backgrounds.

questions.q_en:
Consider the following statements about Indo-Islamic architecture:

I. Muslims borrowed architectural elements liberally from Hindu traditions despite religious differences

II. All Indo-Islamic buildings were constructed primarily for religious purposes

III. Decorative forms included designing on plaster through incision or stucco

IV. Indo-Islamic architecture is a mix of many structural techniques from different cultures

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.solution_en:
Statements I, III, and IV are correct. Muslims absorbed many features of local cultures and traditions and combined them with their own architectural practices. and in spite of the obvious Saracenic, Persian and Turkish influences, Indo-Islamic structures were heavily influenced by prevailing sensibilities of Indian architectural and decorative forms.

Statement II is incorrect. Not all Indo-Islamic buildings were religious; many were forts, palaces, tombs, and public structures like stepwells and caravanserais.

questions.q_en:
Arrange the following phases in the development of Indo-Islamic architecture in chronological order:

I. Development of Provincial Styles in Gujarat and Bengal

II. Initial Muslim constructions in Sind and Gujarat

III. Large-scale building under the Delhi Sultanate

IV. Development of the Mughal Style in Delhi, Agra and Lahore
questions.solution_en:
Initial Muslim constructions in Sind and Gujarat (8th - 12th century CE)

o Early mosques and tombs were built after the Arab conquest of Sind (712 CE) and early Turkish presence in Gujarat.

Large-scale building under the Delhi Sultanate (13th - 15th century CE)

o The Delhi Sultans (Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi dynasties) built Qutb Minar, Alai Darwaza, and Tughlaqabad Fort, marking the first major phase of Indo-Islamic architecture.

Development of Provincial Styles in Gujarat and Bengal (15th century CE)

o As regional kingdoms grew, distinct architectural styles emerged in Gujarat, Bengal, Malwa, and Deccan, blending local influences with Islamic elements.

Development of the Mughal Style in Delhi, Agra, and Lahore (16th - 18th century CE)

o The Mughal emperors (Babur to Aurangzeb) introduced grand structures like Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, Taj Mahal, and Red Fort, blending Persian, Timurid, and Indian architectural elements.

questions.q_en:
Identify the correct statement.

A. A form of stambha or tower that was a common feature in the sub-continent was the minar.

B. The everyday use of the minar was for the azaan or call to prayer.
questions.solution_en:
• A form of stambha or tower that was a common feature in the sub-continent was the minar.

• Two most striking minars of medieval times are the Qutub Minar in Delhi and the Chand Minar at Daulatabad Fort.

• The everyday use of the minar was for the azaan or call to prayer. Its phenomenal height, however, symbolised the might and power of the ruler.

• The Qutub Minar also came to be associated with the much revered saint of Delhi, Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki. The Qutub Minar, built in the thirteenth century, is a 234-feet-high tapering tower divided into five storeys. The minar is a mix of polygonal and circular shapes. It is largely built of red and buff sandstone with some use of marble in the upper storeys. It is characterised by highly decorated balconies and bands of inscriptions intertwined with foliated designs.

• Chand Minar, built in the fifteenth century, is a 210- feet-high tapering tower divided into four storeys. Painted peach now, its façade once boasted of chevron patterning on the encaustic tile work and bold bands of Quranic verses. Although it looked like an Iranian monument, it was the combined handiwork of local architects with those from Delhi and Iran.

questions.q_en: Who built the Jahaaz Mahal in Mandu?
questions.solution_en:
• Jahaaz Mahal is an elegant two-storey 'shippalace' between two reservoirs, with open pavilions, balconies overhanging the water and a terrace. Built by Sultan Ghiyasuddin Khilji it was possibly used as his harem and as the ultimate pleasure and recreational resort. It had a complex arrangement of watercourses and a terrace swimming pool.

Further information:

Mandu is a typical respresentation of the medieval provincial style of art and architecture.

• The city of Mandu is located sixty miles from Indore, at an elevation of over 2000 feet and overlooks the Malwa Plateau to the north and the Narmada valley to the south.

• Mandu's natural defence encouraged consistent habitations by Parmara Rajputs, Afghans and Mughals.

• As the capital city of Ghauri Dynasty (1401 - 1561) founded by Hoshang Shah it acquired a lot of fame. Subsequently, Mandu was associated with the romance of Sultan Baz Bahadur and Rani Rupmati. The Mughals resorted to it for pleasure during the monsoon season.

• It was a complex mix of official and residential-cum-pleasure palace, pavilions, mosques, artificial reservoirs, baolis, embattlements, etc. In spite of the size or monumentality, the structures were very close to nature, designed in the style of arched pavilions, light and airy, so that these buildings did not retain heat. Local stone and marble were used to great advantage. Mandu is a fine example of architectural adaptation to the environment.

• The Royal Enclave located in the city comprised the most complete and romantic set of buildings, a cluster of palaces and attendant structures, official and residential, built around two artificial lakes.

• The Hindola Mahal looks like a railway viaduct bridge with its disproportionately large buttresses supporting the walls. This was the audience hall of the Sultan and also the place where he showed himself to his subjects. Batter was used very effectively to give an impression of swinging (Hindola) walls.

• Jahaaz Mahal is an elegant two-storey 'shippalace' between two reservoirs, with open pavilions, balconies overhanging the water and a terrace. Built by Sultan Ghiyasuddin Khilji it was possibly used as his harem and as the ultimate pleasure and recreational resort. It had a complex arrangement of watercourses and a terrace swimming pool.

• Rani Rupmati's double pavilion perched on the southern embattlements afforded a beautiful view of the Narmada valley. Baz Bahadur's palace had a wide courtyard ringed with halls and terraces.

• A madrasa called Asharfi Mahal now lies in ruins. Hoshang Shah's tomb is a majestic structure with a beautiful dome, marble jali work, porticos, courts and towers. It is regarded as an example of the robustness of Afghan structures, but its lattice work, carved brackets and toranas lend it a softer hue.

• The Jama Masjid of Mandu was built on a large scale to accommodate many worshippers for Friday prayers. It is entered through a monumental gateway, topped with a squat dome, beyond which lies an open courtyard flanked with columned cloisters on three sides, also topped with smaller domes. The building is faced with red sandstone.

• The mimbar in the Qibla Liwan is supported on carved brackets and the mihrab has a lotus bud fringe. Provincial style architecture of Mandu is regarded as too close to the structures of Imperial Delhi to make a bold statement of local traditions.

• Nevertheless, the so-called robust, austere Pathan architecture of Mandu with its surface embellishments of jalis, carved brackets, etc., and the lightness of the structures was an important intervention in the narrative of the Indo-Islamic architectural experience.

Local stone and marble were used to great advantage. Mandu is a fine example of architectural adaptation to the environment.

• The Royal Enclave located in the city comprised the most complete and romantic set of buildings, a cluster of palaces and attendant structures, official and residential, built around two artificial lakes.

• The Hindola Mahal looks like a railway viaduct bridge with its disproportionately large buttresses supporting the walls. This was the audience hall of the Sultan and also the place where he showed himself to his subjects. Batter was used very effectively to give an impression of swinging (Hindola) walls.

• Jahaaz Mahal is an elegant two-storey 'shippalace' between two reservoirs, with open pavilions, balconies overhanging the water and a terrace. Built by Sultan Ghiyasuddin Khilji it was possibly used as his harem and as the ultimate pleasure and recreational resort. It had a complex arrangement of watercourses and a terrace swimming pool.

• Rani Rupmati's double pavilion perched on the southern embattlements afforded a beautiful view of the Narmada valley. Baz Bahadur's palace had a wide courtyard ringed with halls and terraces.

• A madrasa called Asharfi Mahal now lies in ruins. Hoshang Shah's tomb is a majestic structure with a beautiful dome, marble jali work, porticos, courts and towers. It is regarded as an example of the robustness of Afghan structures, but its lattice work, carved brackets and toranas lend it a softer hue.

• The Jama Masjid of Mandu was built on a large scale to accommodate many worshippers for Friday prayers. It is entered through a monumental gateway, topped with a squat dome, beyond which lies an open courtyard flanked with columned cloisters on three sides, also topped with smaller domes. The building is faced with red sandstone.

• The mimbar in the Qibla Liwan is supported on carved brackets and the mihrab has a lotus bud fringe. Provincial style architecture of Mandu is regarded as too close to the structures of Imperial Delhi to make a bold statement of local traditions.

• Nevertheless, the so-called robust, austere Pathan architecture of Mandu with its surface embellishments of jalis, carved brackets, etc., and the lightness of the structures was an important intervention in the narrative of the Indo-Islamic architectural experience.
